To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) a federal government can influence the composition of the provincial tax structure by means of conditional lump-sum grants, (ii) a federal government may use matching grants to induce a province to increase its spending in a particular area, and (iii) the federal government can use matching grants to reduce provincial spending in a particular sector.
the equilibrium grants structure is a function of political and economic variables and that the role of conditional lump-sum grants and matching grants are different.

the equilibrium grants structure is determined by the relative size of the federal government and the extent of the disagreement between the federal government and provincial governments, and that the relative size of federal and provincial governments, as well as the extent of disagreement between them, determine the pattern of social expenditure by provincial governments and the composition of tax burdens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the political economy of intergovernmental relations.
the effects of shocks on the equilibrium pattern of intergovernmental transfers, which in turn affect the pattern of public expenditure.
explaining the observed evolution of the Canadian intergovernmental transfer system in terms of political shocks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the grants system is a complex and dynamic phenomenon, which is determined by the interplay of political, economic and institutional factors, and that the theory of grants has to take this complexity and dynamics into account.
matching grants are a means of influencing provincial or state spending, and lump-sum grants are a means for influencing the tax structure..
grants are a tool of federalism, and the design of grants reflects the underlying political economy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
grants are a tool to influence the pattern and composition of public spending and tax burden across levels of government.
grants are used as a tool for redistribution across the levels of governments and across the provinces.
the structure of intergovernmental fiscal grants is determined by the relative bargaining power of the federal and provincial governments and the degree of fiscal decentralization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of intergovernmental transfers is a complex and dynamic process that is affected by many political and economic factors.
grants can be used to induce cooperation between the levels of government and, in particular, to induce a more efficient pattern of public spending.
the grants structure is a tool that the federal government can use to achieve its political goals.
